title: The treadle pump

paragraphs.text: Until now, governments and development agencies have tried to tackle the problem of managing water supplies for irrigation through large-scale projects: gigantic dams, sprawling irrigation canals and vast new fields of high-yield crops introduced during the Green Revolution, the famous campaign to increase grain harvests in developing nations that took place between 1940 and 1960. Traditional irrigation, however, has degraded the soil in many areas, and the reservoirs behind dams can quickly fill up with silt, reducing their storage capacity and depriving downstream farmers of fertile sediments. Furthermore, although the Green Revolution has greatly expanded worldwide farm production since 1950, poverty stubbornly persists in parts of Africa, Asia and Latin America. Continued improvements in the productivity of large farms may play the main role in boosting food supply, but local efforts to provide cheap, individual irrigation systems for small farms may offer a better way to lift people out of poverty.

Abdul Rahman, a farmer in the Noakhali district of Bangladesh, has a three-quarter acre plot of rain-fed rice fields. In 1981, Abdul could grow only 700 kilograms of rice each year — 300 kilograms less than what he needed to feed his family. During the three months before the October rice harvests came in, Abdul and his wife had to watch while their children survived on one meal a day or less. When asked what he needed to move out of poverty, he said, ‘control of water for my crops, at a price I can afford.’

simple device that succeeded in helping Abdul achieve his goal is the treadle pump. The treadle pump is a kind of water technology designed, manufactured and marketed with smallholders in mind. It is a simple, low-cost, manual (foot-operated) pump that can lift water from shallow groundwater sources or surface water bodies. The typical pump consists of two vertical cylinders fitted with pistons. The operator stands on the treadles and uses a stepping motion. As one treadle is pushed down the other treadle comes up. Vertical posts attached to the treadles and cut from bamboo are used to balance the operator.

Basic treadle pumps can lift groundwater from depths of up to seven meters with a flow rate ranging from about 30 to 80 liters per minute depending on the rigor of the operator, water depth and cylinder diameter. Leg muscles are used in a natural walking motion, making it possible for an operator to pump continuously for several hours per day delivering enough water to irrigate roughly half an acre of vegetables. It costs only $25 (including the cost of drilling a tube well down to the groundwater).

Developed in the late 1970s by Norwegian engineer Gunnar Barnes, the pumps are so simple that local craftsmen can manufacture them using readily available tools and materials; and they can be maintained and repaired easily by the users. Parts requiring periodic replacement, such as the plastic piston seals, which are common to many popular hand pumps, are usually available in local markets, and the foot valve is made from rubber that can be replaced using a discarded bicycle tire.

Abdul heard about the treadle pump from a cousin and was one of the first farmers in Bangladesh to buy one. He borrowed the money from an uncle and easily repaid the loan four months later. During the five-month dry season, when Bangladeshis typically farm very little, Abdul used the treadle pump to grow chilli peppers, tomatoes, cabbage and eggplants. He also improved the yield of one of his rice plots by irrigating it. His family ate some of the vegetables and sold the rest at the village market, earning a net profit of $100. With his new income, Abdul was able to buy rice for his family to eat, keep his two sons in school until they were 16 and set aside a little money for his daughter’s dowry. Within a few years, he had doubled the size of his vegetable plot and changed the thatched roof on his house for one made of corrugated tin. His family was raising a calf and some chickens.

Bangladesh is particularly well suited for the treadle pump because a huge reservoir of groundwater lies just a few meters below the farmers’ feet. In the early 1980s, IDE (International Development Enterprises) initiated a campaign to market the pump, encouraging 75 small private-sector companies to manufacture the devices and several thousand village dealers and tube-well drillers to sell and install them. Over the next 12 years, one and a half million farm families purchased treadle pumps, which increased the farmers’ net income by a total of $150 million a year. The cost of IDE’s market-creation activities was only $12 million, leveraged by the investment of $37.5 million from the farmers themselves. In contrast, the expense of building a conventional dam and canal system to irrigate an equivalent area of farmland would be in the range of $2000 per acre, or $1.5 billion. In terms of reducing poverty, the treadle pump has proved superior to more technologically advanced irrigation schemes.
